what_its_for: Azathioprine is used to suppress your immune system. It is most commonly used to prevent your body from rejecting a transplanted organ (such as a kidney). It is also used to treat certain autoimmune conditions where your immune system mistakenly attacks your own body, such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis), and other conditions.
how_to_take: Take azathioprine exactly as your doctor prescribes. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Take it WITH food or milk to help reduce stomach upset and nausea. Try to take it at the same time each day to keep a steady level in your body. Do not crush, break, or chew the tablets. If you handle broken tablets, avoid touching your face and wash your hands thoroughly, as the drug can be absorbed through the skin.
dosing: Your dose is carefully calculated based on your body weight, the condition being treated, your kidney and liver function, and how your body responds to the medicine. Doses vary widely from person to person. Never change your dose on your own. Your doctor will start you at a certain dose and may adjust it over time based on lab results and how you are doing. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — BUT only if it is still the same day. If it is already the next day or almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose completely and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store azathioprine at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from light, heat, and moisture. Do NOT store it in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a safe medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick or have infections, as azathioprine weakens your immune system and makes it harder to fight illness. Avoid live vaccines (such as the shingles vaccine Zostavax, MMR, or yellow fever vaccine) while taking this medicine — talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines. Limit sun exposure and wear sunscreen and protective clothing outdoors, as this medicine increases your risk of skin cancer. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice. Do NOT take allopurinol (Zyloprim, used for gout) without telling your doctor first, as this combination can cause a serious and dangerous increase in azathioprine levels in your body. Avoid alcohol unless your doctor says it is okay.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: unusual bruising or bleeding, signs of infection (fever, chills, sore throat, cough, painful urination), severe nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), unusual tiredness or weakness, dark urine or pale stools, new skin changes, sores, or growths, or shortness of breath. Also contact your doctor promptly if you feel generally unwell or something does not feel right. This medicine requires regular blood tests (complete blood count and liver function tests) to watch for serious side effects — do not miss your lab appointments.
when_it_works: Azathioprine does not work overnight. For transplant patients, it begins working right away to help prevent rejection, but you must keep taking it every day. For autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease, it may take 6 to 12 weeks or even longer — sometimes up to 3 to 6 months — before you notice improvement in your symptoms. Be patient and do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor, even if you do not feel better right away.
special_populations: PREGNANCY: Azathioprine may harm an unborn baby. Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or become pregnant while taking this medicine. Both men and women of childbearing age should discuss effective contraception with their doctor while taking azathioprine. BREASTFEEDING: This medicine may pass into breast milk. Do not breastfeed while taking azathioprine without first talking to your doctor. KIDNEY OR LIVER PROBLEMS: Your dose may need to be adjusted if you have kidney or liver disease. Make sure your doctor knows your full medical history. GENETIC TESTING: Some people have a genetic variation that makes them break down azathioprine differently, which can increase the risk of serious side effects. Your doctor may order a blood test (TPMT or NUDT15 enzyme test) before starting this medicine to determine the safest dose for you. ELDERLY PATIENTS: Older adults may be more sensitive to the effects of this medicine and may require closer monitoring.
